cases.final_diagnosis: CNC-02 has a genuine running mechanical fault: vibration remains around 4.2-4.58 mm/s and repeatedly crosses the 4.50 mm/s alarm threshold (alarms at ticks 914 and 919; values above 4.50 at ticks 922, 926 and 928 in the 920-930 window, max 4.577 mm/s over 900-920). Separately, CNC-04 shows an independent mechanical change: vibration stepped up around tick 909 from under 0.5 mm/s during ticks 900-908 to roughly 1.7-2.4 mm/s through tick 930. CNC-05, CNC-06, CNC-07 and CNC-08 are running with stable normal vibration; CNC-01 and CNC-03 are idle and were not measured. This is not instrument noise: crossings continued after tick 920.

Pending further discrimination between H1 (batch-2 material defect) and H2 (CNC-05/CNC-06 machine fault). All three failed jobs (11-13, batch 2) had CNC-06 as their last machine before inspection (E4, E5). CNC-06 vibration mean is 2.19 mm/s in 1082-1216 (E12) versus CNC-01 peer mean 1.81 mm/s in the same window (E13); CNC-05 mean 2.06 mm/s in 1023-1148 (E9) versus CNC-01 mean 1.73 mm/s (E10). CNC-03 and CNC-04 vibration remain unchecked, and no events log check for material/setting changes has been done. CNC-02 (hydraulics) mean 1.94 mm/s (E14) may not be a comparable baseline. Confidence not yet at the 0.90 intervention threshold.

CNC-01 experienced a transient vibration exceedance above the 4.50 mm/s alarm threshold for four consecutive ticks (521: 7.01, 522: 7.25, 523: 7.19, 524: 7.37 mm/s; E5, corroborated by E4/E13 with max 7.374 mm/s over ticks 515-524) while running job 8, which started at tick 475 and has no logged operation/tool/feed change at 521-524 (E11; E5). Vibration then returned to baseline (max 2.416, mean 2.288 mm/s over ticks 525-530; E13) and CNC-01 is still running (E3). All other machines were normal in the same window: CNC-02 max 2.22, CNC-04 max 2.37, CNC-06 max 2.65, CNC-05 max 2.25 mm/s, and idle CNC-03 near zero at ticks 529-530 (E7-E12). No process event explains the spike, so H2 is ruled out. The clean four-tick pulse with full recovery is most consistent with a transient mechanical disturbance (loose workpiece/tooling or resonance) that self-resolved (H1). A vibration-channel sensor fault (H3) cannot be fully excluded because every supporting measurement comes from the same CNC-01 vibration channel, but it is less parsimonious given the pulse shape and recovery. No persistent fault is indicated.

CNC-03 experienced a transient mechanical vibration exceedance at ticks 381-383 (alarms of 6.78, 6.84, 6.78 mm/s against a 4.50 mm/s threshold; E4 shows a 6.83673 mm/s peak in 375-390) that has resolved. CNC-03 is now idle (load near 0 since tick 393, E14) with vibration at 0.22 mm/s (E16) and no active alarm. There is no evidence of a current fault on CNC-03 or a line-wide cause: peer machines CNC-01 and CNC-02 ran normally through the same window (E10, E13) and factory air temperature was normal (E9). The root cause of the transient is not identified, but no component-level fault is presently indicated. H2 (sensor fault) and H3 (nuisance alarm) are contradicted by the consistent, threshold-exceeding readings (E4, E8, E19); H4 (common cause) is contradicted by the normal peers and air temperature (E10, E13, E9).

CNC-03 experienced a transient high-vibration event at ticks 71-78: vibration jumped to about 5.0-5.21 mm/s (above the 4.50 mm/s alarm threshold, eight consecutive alarms) while the machine was idle and unloaded. The event has cleared: from tick 80 through the present tick 90, CNC-03 vibration is normal (ticks 80-90: max 0.3555 mm/s, mean 0.1408 mm/s). During the event, CNC-03 power was normal (ticks 70-78: 1.64-2.35 kW, mean 1.987 kW) and almost identical to idle comparison machine CNC-04 (mean 1.983 kW), while CNC-04 itself showed only near-zero vibration (max 0.386 mm/s, ticks 70-78). So an electrical or idle-power cause (H3) is ruled out. The leading explanation is a transient vibration-sensor failure that cleared by tick 80 (H1): the readings jumped to ~5 mm/s and back to near zero abruptly while the machine sat idle with no load. However, a self-clearing intermittent mechanical fault (H2) cannot be excluded with the tools available, because no sensor-swap test (T1) or independent accelerometer/direct inspection (T2) can be performed.

CNC-04 has a progressive feed-axis fault (worn axis servo drive or binding axis), unique to CNC-04. In ticks 1120-1130 its following_error ran 17.96-20.26 µm (mean 18.92) and hit 20.26 µm at tick 1129, tripping the 20 µm alarm, while CNC-01/02/03/05 all stayed at roughly 3-5 µm (means 3.62-4.94) in the same window. CNC-04's error has been rising for a long time (about 13 µm mean in 1000-1059, about 16.8 µm in 1060-1119, about 18.9 µm in 1120-1130), its power is steady around 12.4 kW, and it has no hydraulics, so this is not overload, not a line-wide cause, and not a job-14 transient. H4 is contradicted by the other four stations being low; H3 is contradicted by the pre-existing progressive rise before job 14 started at 1098.

CNC-02's axis servo drive (or its amplifier) is degrading. Its following_error has risen steadily from a ~13.7 µm mean at ticks 1200-1219 to ~19.0 µm at ticks 1340-1359, exceeding the 20.00 µm alarm limit (max 20.103 µm in that bucket; still ~19-20.2 µm at tick 1370 with no recovery after a 10-tick wait). The fault is confined to CNC-02: CNC-01, CNC-03, CNC-04, CNC-06 and CNC-07 all run at roughly 2-6 µm over the same period, and CNC-02's vibration, power, temperature and load are flat (E6, E11, E12, E17), which argues against mechanical drive-train wear (H2, which would raise load/vibration) and against a factory-wide problem. The error did not self-recover (E16), making a transient or purely controller-tuning fault (H3) unlikely. Mechanical wear cannot be fully excluded without a physical inspection, but it is a weak alternative given the flat load and vibration. The single earlier inspection failure (job 11, batch 2, tick 1143, E13) predates the error rise and is not explained by this fault.

CNC-05 has a real internal hydraulic fault — a leaking seal, weakening pump, or sticking relief valve — causing pressure to fall even while the station is idle. CNC-05 hydraulic pressure declined from a mean of 61.355 bar (ticks 1100-1129) to 54.29 bar at the alarm near tick 1281, with continuous samples through tick 1290 (E4, E7), so this is not missing data from a switched-off machine. CNC-05 sat idle but powered during the decline, and per the manual (E2) a pressure fall that persists while idle is a leak, not a heavy cut or transducer error. CNC-02, the only other hydraulics-equipped machine, stays flat at about 69 bar across the same window (E3, E5), so the shared supply is healthy and the fault is isolated to CNC-05. CNC-05 has run no parts recently, so reject-share evidence is unavailable rather than contradictory (E6). Confidence 0.90. H1 supported; H2 (branch restriction) remains possible but points to the same repair on CNC-05 and is not needed to decide.

CNC-02 has an intermittent hydraulic restriction (sticking valve or partially clogged filter) causing transient pressure drops below the 55 bar setpoint — a physical fault localized to CNC-02, not a one-off sensor glitch and not normal load draw. Hydraulic pressure fell to 54.46 bar at tick 1041 (the alarm) and a second sub-55 dip, 54.90 bar, recurred at tick 1052, with full recovery between dips and pressure back to 59.18 bar at tick 1050. Load was already high and steady (~48 bar) from tick 1035 with no spike at 1041, vibration stayed normal, inspections passed, and sibling hydraulic machine CNC-05 stayed stable around 66-71 bar with no dips, so CNC-01, CNC-03, CNC-04, CNC-06 and CNC-05 show no matching fault.
